content: Smallpox is a highly contagious disease that exclusively affects humans. It is caused by two variants of the variola virus: Variola major and Variola minor. Variola major is the more severe form, with a mortality rate of 30–35%, while Variola minor causes a milder disease known as alastrim, which has a mortality rate of approximately 1%. Survivors of smallpox often bear long-term consequences, including characteristic skin scarring. In some cases, complications such as blindness due to corneal ulcerations and infertility in male survivors may occur. Historically, smallpox has had a profound impact on human civilization. The disease is believed to be at least 16,000 years old and has significantly influenced the history of Europe, Asia, North America, and Africa. The earliest clinical evidence of smallpox was identified in the mummified remains of the Egyptian Pharaoh Ramses V. Smallpox has also been weaponized throughout history, with the most recent example being its use during World War II. Following extensive vaccination campaigns in the 19th and 20th centuries, the World Health Organization (WHO) certified the eradication of smallpox in 1980. The eradication of smallpox was officially declared by the WHO in 1980, marking the culmination of a global effort. This achievement required significant financial investment and years of coordinated international action, as all countries were vulnerable to the devastating effects of the disease. After the last known death from smallpox in 1978, which occurred due to an accidental laboratory exposure, all known stocks of the virus were destroyed, except for those retained for research purposes. Currently, the only remaining stocks of the variola virus are held in secure laboratories at the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and the Russian State Research Center of Virology and Biotechnology (VECTOR). The smallpox virus can be transmitted through contaminated surfaces or aerosolized particles. It evades the host's immune system and replicates within host cells, causing three potential forms of the disease: ordinary smallpox, flat-type smallpox, and hemorrhagic smallpox. The virus infects various cell types in the body and is characterized by its distinctive skin lesions. Smallpox is caused by the variola virus, a double-stranded DNA virus belonging to the Poxviridae family. There are two forms of the virus, each with differing levels of virulence, as evidenced by their respective mortality rates. The virus is resilient in cold and aerosolized environments, which facilitates its transmission via respiratory droplets among humans, its only host species. Unlike other DNA viruses, the variola virus replicates in the cytoplasm of host cells, demonstrating a unique tropism. Before its eradication, smallpox needed to be distinguished from other diseases that cause vesicular rashes and fever, such as chickenpox (which was often mistaken for smallpox), herpes zoster, and erythema multiforme. The true incidence of smallpox prior to its eradication in 1980 is difficult to determine due to underreporting, particularly in endemic regions. It is estimated that reported cases represented only 1–2% of the actual number of infections. Children and young adults were the most affected populations, especially in areas with low levels of immunity. There was no evidence of gender or racial differences in disease incidence, but developing countries experienced higher rates of infection. Individuals at risk of contracting smallpox included laboratory workers handling the virus and those living in areas targeted by bioterrorism. Before eradication, risk factors included direct physical contact with infected individuals, exposure to contaminated bodily fluids, and inhalation of aerosolized particles. The natural progression of smallpox typically begins with flu-like symptoms, followed by the development of a skin rash. The rash progresses in a characteristic manner, eventually forming scabs that fall off, leaving scars. Complications may include respiratory conditions such as bronchitis or pneumonia, as well as joint, bone, or eye involvement. The overall fatality rate for the Variola major form of smallpox was approximately 30%. The diagnosis of smallpox was guided by an algorithm developed by the CDC, which relied on specific major and minor criteria. Symptoms of smallpox followed a predictable pattern and commonly included high fever, a rash (initially appearing in the oral mucosa and later spreading to the skin), malaise, fatigue, muscle pain, and vomiting. Physical examination findings varied depending on the stage of the disease and could include high fever, tachycardia secondary to fever, oral mucosal rash, skin rash with a typical progression, ophthalmological changes, abdominal pain, and altered mental status. Laboratory confirmation involved polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing and the growth of the virus in specific cell cultures. There is no antiviral treatment for smallpox. Management focuses on supportive care, including hydration, administration of medications to reduce fever and pain, and treatment of secondary bacterial or viral infections. Primary prevention of smallpox involves the administration of the vaccinia vaccine, which can attenuate or suppress disease manifestations if given shortly after exposure. In the absence of an outbreak, the vaccine is only administered to clinical or laboratory workers handling the virus in specialized facilities. However, the vaccine has several adverse effects, particularly in immunosuppressed individuals, those with heart conditions, or those with allergies, necessitating careful administration under specific guidelines. In the event of a smallpox outbreak, the CDC has developed a series of measures to protect the population. The eradication of smallpox was a cost-effective public health achievement, as the disease was successfully eliminated in 1980. Despite its eradication, ongoing research aims to develop antiviral drugs against the smallpox virus due to the potential for an outbreak or its use in bioterrorism.
